newsitem.title: UK: Fatty oils diet may relieve dyslexia, dyspraxia.
newsitem.headline: Fatty oils diet may relieve dyslexia, dyspraxia.

text.p: By Neil Winton, Science and Technology Correspondent
Children suffering from dyslexia, dyspraxia and hyperactivity can often be helped by a supplement of fatty acids to their diet, experts said on Wednesday.
A lack of essential fatty acids in modern diets was a likely cause of dyslexia and reading difficulties, dyspraxia's extreme clumsiness and the unsociable behaviour of the hyperactive child.

Dr Jackie Stordy of the University of Surrey told a news conference test results showed that clumsy children treated with a combination of essential lipids with thyme oil, which promotes the incorporation of these lipids into the brain and eye, made a noticeable improvement in manual dexterity after three months.
Lipids are fats which make up cell membranes and regulate almost all cell functions.

The news conference was organised by Efamol, a subsidiary of Scotia Holdings Plc, which produces the dietary supplement for this treatment. Its product, Efalex, contains tuna oil, evening primrose oil, vitamin E and thyme oil.
Dr Basant Puri, from London's Hammersmith Hospital, said dyslexic brains show differences in cell structure.
"Dyslexics are poor at processing very rapid changes in visual stimulation and contribute to the perceptual disturbances that many dyslexics describe when trying to read," Puri said.
But Puri said precise reasons had not yet been discovered.
Puri's researches were undertaken with a magnetic resonance spectroscope brain-scanner at Hammersmith hoipstial.
Dyslexics are found across the whole range of intelligence. It is often inherited. Children affected have difficulty reading, writing, and spelling. They often confuse right and left, time and tense.
Dyspraxics find it difficult to catch balls, and lack a sense of direction, position or time. They have poor concentration and memory.
Hyperactive children are often impulsive and crave immediate satisfaction. They can be irritated by touch, smells and sounds, and suffer stress from new or unpredictable situations.
Some children show symptons across all three categories.
Stordy said dyspraxic children taking a fatty acid supplement had improved measurably after three months.

"They were so much calmer and able to cope with stress so much better. Their skills of manual dexterity, ball skills and static and dynamic balance were still worse than average children, but they were just not so serious," Stordy said.

Dr David Horrobin, chief executive of Scotia Holdings, said a mother's natural breast milk helped make sure infants received a healthy foundation of essential fatty acids. Infant formula did not provide this part of the diet.
Horrobin said until the 1950s in Britain, children were routinely given cod liver oil as part of their diet.
"Since this stopped, we've seen an increase in these problems. We are now getting a generation of mothers who are not passing on essential fatty acids to their offspring," he said.
But breast feeding was not a guarantee against dyslexia.
"If you are genetically not well endowed with fatty acids, breast feeding will not be enough. You will need a supplement to build them up," Stordy said.
